paras: Every review is positive, and most describe a balanced, power-leaning hybrid, with two placing it just below the Selkirk Boomstick for power. Reviewers disagree on control: one found the pop hard to control until weight was added, while another calls it the most forgiving paddle in a four-way comparison, though with less spin than grittier options. Testing ran from a few days to about two months.

Reviewers describe a mid-to-high power hybrid that suits intermediate and advanced players, most often measured against the 11SIX24 Power 2 or its elongated sibling, the J6CR. They disagree on control: some call it easy to keep in play, while one mixed take finds the pop tricky to control, needing a week or two and added weight to settle. Another mixed take dislikes the short handle and throat taper, and one reviewer's first unit arrived with weak grit, a problem another says others have reported.

Many reviewers treat it as an upgrade on the original Coral, with a little more power and spin but a crisper, firmer feel, and several note it is UPA approved only. It suits all-court and control-first players, roughly 3.0 to 4.5 by one reviewer. Two of the three mixed takes say it is too low on power and unstable off-center for singles or top-level play (Rackets & Runners), or plays as a power paddle with little dwell that lower-level players may not enjoy (SupaSenpai).

Most note it runs heavy for a hybrid, and reviewers mostly compare it with the Bread & Butter Loco, with several saying it pops less. The one mixed review, from Pickleball3en, found volley rolls at the kitchen popped too much, so pop is where they disagree. The five who checked found little grit wear.

No review is negative, and many pitch the paddle at beginners, newer players and anyone who struggles with control, often as a strong value under $100. The usual caveat is that power and pop are modest, and several say it cannot match thermoformed paddles. Reviewers split on the thin 14mm version, with two rejecting it and two praising it, and the Hyperion is the most common comparison.

Nikki Maldonado calls it the ultimate soft game paddle for doubles but not a singles paddle, and says drives need extra effort. Pickleball Studio, The Pickleball Dad, Pickleball Effect and Johnkew Pickleball each say it is not for players who want maximum power or aggression. Johnkew, Matt's Pickleball and Pickleball Effect all rate the Power 2 Pegasus ahead of it on power.

Pickle Bill, Matthew K Pickleball and Pickleball Effect praise its forgiving sweet spot, and the first two add that control is its strength, with Matthew K recommending it to learners and control lovers. Drill More Pickleball, the one negative take, found the wide body too poppy at the kitchen and prefers the Ultre, and Pickleball Tech Dude calls the area above the corners a dead zone.

Reviewers mostly praise the Ultre Power 2 for elite spin, easy power and a large sweet spot, with Pickleball Playbook and Pickleheads pointing it at intermediate and better players. Mixed takes come from control and touch: Pickleball On Call rated control 3.5 out of 10 for both Power 2 shapes and called the sweet spot hit or miss, and Matt's Pickleball gave it the lowest control score of three paddles, while Farmer Lanky Pickleball found the sweet spot very forgiving. West Side Pickleball narrowly preferred the Bread and Butter Loco 2 at nearly the same price, and several reviewers say drops and resets need care.

highlights.text: found the sweet spot very forgiving
lowest control score of three paddles

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the spin and a grit surface that held up in long tests, with Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Effect both running wear tests where the grit held up. Mixed takes come from Famous by Friday, who found occasional flyers and a break-in period, and Pickle Li, who got weak spin in stock form until weight was added. Power is mostly rated mid-tier, so several reviewers added weight, and a number of reviewers note the face is UPA only, which some tournaments do not allow.

highlights.text: a grit surface that held up
occasional flyers and a break-in period

paras: Reviewers mostly praise it as a spin-heavy elongated foam paddle with a large sweet spot, suited to intermediate and advanced players who are comfortable with power and willing to tune it, and several add tape to raise the low swing weight. Power rankings differ: Pickleheads puts it among the strongest paddles they have seen, Pickleball Effect places it mid range below the Boomstick and Loco, and Ignatowich HQ gives a mixed take, finding it a step below the Loco with resets never fully comfortable. Grit is partly a version question, as STS Pickleball measured about 1 percent spin loss over 100 games on the Crystal Blue Endurance edition, while Johnkew Pickleball found the standard peel ply surface wears over weeks or months.

Reviewers praise the power, spin and dense, stable feel, with Pickleball Union and Pickleheads pointing it at intermediate to advanced aggressive players rather than beginners. Takes split on thickness: Johnkew Pickleball and Pickleball Medicine found the 16 mm easier to control, while Pickleball Studio and Rackets & Runners preferred the 14 mm for resets and depth control. Pickleball Studio called the update from the 3S minor and JJ Pickleball saw no reason to upgrade unless the USAP stamp matters, while Pickleball Willy and Johnkew Pickleball questioned $280 next to cheaper options and Rackets & Runners and Johnkew Pickleball said durability needs time.

Reviewers disagree on where it sits. Womack Pickleball and Pickleball Pursuit call it all court, Pickleball Medicine rates the series best for control, and JJ Pickleball classes it as a lower end power paddle. Six reviewers call the E shape niche, narrow or unstable, and five mention a break-in that changes the feel, with Johnkew telling control players to wait.

Many reviewers praise its power, with Pickleball Blast putting it level with or above the Selkirk Boomstick. Several limit it to advanced or aggressive players: Ignatowich HQ, Matt's Pickleball, Pickleball Effect and West Side Pickleball, which sets 4.0 to 4.5 as the minimum. The two negative takes, a West Side video and a Pickleball Paddle Reviews TikTok, call it high risk or very hard to control.

Reviewers mostly praise it as an all-court control paddle with a large, forgiving sweet spot, with Womack Pickleball calling it probably the best all-court paddle tested this year and Pickleheads logging 25 plus hours with the surface looking nearly new. Feel is where takes split: Smash Pickleball found it almost squishy and hard to read on dinks, while Johnkew Pickleball calls it plush and arm friendly and The Sweet Spot Pickleball notes feel is subjective. Power is the other limit, as Pickleball_Ace, Matt's Pickleball and Johnkew Pickleball all place it below the Boomstick, and Pickleball Playbook preferred the hybrid after the elongated player shanked about every fifth ball.

Despite the control label, Pickleball Studio calls it a power paddle, and Pickleball Effect finds more pop than a typical raw carbon paddle. Pickleball Studio would not recommend it to players who struggle with resets. The one mixed take, from Pickleball Effect, did not take to it right away and added lead tape for a plusher feel, comparing it with the Carbon X series. Mid-Century Pickleball argues all court paddles suit players moving up levels.

Many reviewers praise its spin and control. Womack Pickleball, the one negative review, found a small sweet spot with a significant drop in pop and power off center and finds it hard to recommend at $200. Pickleball Tech Dude says the sweet spot needs a lot of weight modification, and Famous by Friday Pickleball says it is begging for weight.

Many reviewers praise its spin, with several measuring over 2,000 RPM. Pickleball Pursuit, one of the two mixed takes, saw the grit lose spin after about 3 to 4 hours and prefers the J2K, and the other, Pickleball Effect, still controls the Double Black Diamond better. Pickleball Studio and Dash Pickleball say Double Black Diamond owners need not upgrade.

Matthew K Pickleball calls it a strong choice for control lovers, but Pickleball Medicine, Pickleball Pursuit, STS Pickleball and All Drive No Drop Pickleball place it in the all court category. Six reviewers compare its play with the Volair Mach 2 Forza, and five of them find the Forza more controllable. Pickleball Studio finds the stock paddle vibrates and says it needs lead tape to reach its potential.

Many reviewers praise a plush, soft feel and strong spin, and Jordan Plays Pickle named the 16 mm Flash their favorite paddle of the year. UnforcedErrorsPB, in both a review and a TikTok, found the Flash head heavy and sluggish at the kitchen, Pickle Techie found it slow there with little pop, and Pickleheads rated control below the Prism Flash.

highlights.text: a plush, soft feel and strong spin

paras: Dwell Time Pickleball recommends it for players 4.0 and below, and Pickleheads for 3.0 to 4.5, though Pickleheads warns beginners may find the feedback off-putting. The one mixed take, from Matt's Pickleball, found it inconsistent out of the box and recommends it only for players willing to tinker. Four reviewers compare it with the Quanta, and Pickleball Studio finds the Pro more playable out of the box.

highlights.text: more playable out of the box

paras: Reviewers recommend it for fans of the 11six24 shape and players who want reach, a long handle for two-handed backhands and elite spin, with several reporting little grit loss. Two of the mixed reviews call it the least forgiving Power 2 shape, one finds less pop high on the face, and two lean toward the Vapor. Several rate power as mid-tier.

Reviewers describe it as one of the best price-to-performance power paddles, with elite power and a large sweet spot for an elongated shape. One reviewer lists the high stock swing weight as the main con, since it leaves little room for perimeter weight, and had a weight pod fly off the matte edge guard. Three say it is more controllable than the Boomstick, though Johnkew finds it a bit more unpredictable, and several prefer the standard or hybrid shape.

Two reviewers call the standard widebody the standout of the Loco line, and reviewers praise its large, stable sweet spot and value at under $180 with a code. Several measure a stock swing weight near 110, and two say that leaves room for perimeter weight. Two reviewers put its power a little below the Boomstik, and one says it is probably not for players who struggle with elite power paddles.

highlights.text: probably not for players who struggle

paras: Reviewers who like a foam core that shapes spin and still plays soft at the net respond best, with Paddle Addicts calling it the one paddle that does everything. Both mixed takes find the elongated shape less forgiving than other Genesis shapes, and Pickleball Effect says it needs modifications to reach its potential. Three creators prefer the CRBN 2 shape for hand speed or stability.

highlights.text: needs modifications to reach its potential

paras: Most reviewers pick this standard second shape as the best of the series, calling it the most maneuverable and forgiving, and a fit for players who value spin and stability. Several place its power in the lower or middle range. Tickle My Pickleball, the one mixed take, found the first session underwhelming and still prefers the 3X shape.

Reviewers suit it to precision players who value dwell and soft-game control and are willing to tune it, and several call its spin among the best available. Two of the three mixed takes point to the high swing weight, with one finding it clunky and another struggling in hand battles. Several prefer the CRBN 2 shape.

Reviewers praise the dense, connected feel without a hollow echo, along with predictable power and good spin. Power placement varies: Pickleball Blast puts the elongated version at the lower to low mid end of the power category, while Matt's Pickleball measures it at the 89th percentile and says it matches the Loco on power. Forgiveness also splits by shape, with The Pickleball Dad calling the widebody sweet spot best in class, while The Sweet Spot Pickleball and Matt's Pickleball find the elongated less forgiving off center.

Reviewers describe it as strong power for about $100, playing very close to the Luzz Inferno, and suit it to bangers and Gen 3 players who dislike the EPP feel. The one mixed take, from Pickleball Studio, finds soft shots less consistent, warns that MPP paddles disbond more often than EPP ones, and would pick the EPP Turbo. Two other reviewers needed a few games to adjust to the stiff, hollow feel.

Reviewers describe an attacking power paddle, with UnforcedErrorsPB saying the Pro clearly wants to attack and Famous by Friday finding the feel mega plush. Both mixed takes point to the soft game: Johnny Pickleball says resets and blocks needed adjustment, and Matt's Pickleball keeps returning to the regular Aura for easier resets.

Several reviewers prefer the hybrid shape to the elongated GX2 Power, finding it more maneuverable, stable and forgiving, and Matt's Pickleball calls it the clear standout. High dwell time means resets and short shots take practice for three reviewers. Pickleball Studio, the one mixed take, calls it an advanced paddle for 4.5 and above players with a dialed in soft game.

Reviewers mostly compare it with the Perseus Pro 4, and Pickleball Studio prefers it as more predictable and easier to swing. Three place the sweet spot higher on the face, while two find it weaker near the top corners. Three mixed takes cover a niche paddle that punishes low contact, a 14 mm that pops a lot, and $280 for a Gen 3 paddle with an expiration date.

highlights.text: more predictable and easier to swing

paras: Most reviewers like it, with bouncecraft calling it an all-court paddle that is good at doing everything and suits most players. Reviewers split on thickness: both mixed takes prefer the 14mm, while Pickleheads and Paddle Addicts prefer the 16mm for its more cushioned feel. Mid-Century finds the power adequate and on the lower end, and one host would not spend their own money on it.

highlights.text: would not spend their own money

paras: Reviewers see a refinement of the Pro IV more than an upgrade, with a softer feel, less pop and more predictable resets. Several fault the smooth, low-grit face, and three question the $300 price, with Francis Rances calling it a tough sell. Two suggest it for Pro IV fans who want a hybrid shape with more control.

Reviewers credit it with a softer, more controlled feel than the Pro 4, though most of the six mixed takes see only a minor or lateral update. Price is the main sticking point, with several pointing to a discounted Pro 4 or waiting, and one choosing the Honolulu J6CR instead. The one positive take likes it right out of the box.

Reviewers cast it as a cheap Gen 3 power paddle, with Pickleball Willy calling it probably the best power paddle under $100 and several comparing it with the JOOLA Perseus Pro 4. Three of the four mixed takes find the sweet spot small or tight, and Pickleheads sees few beginners using it for lack of forgiveness. Several players added weight or lead tape.

Reviewers praise strong power, heavy grit and a bigger sweet spot, and Pickleball Paddle Reviews picked it as the favorite of three new Luzz paddles. Several say it plays stiff at first and softens with break-in. BK Pickleball tells players at 3.5 or below to stay away until technique improves. One mixed take could not match the $99 Enhance MPP Turbo for power.

Reviewers describe one of the most powerful square paddles on the market with standout spin, and its Gen 1 non-thermoformed build lowers core crush worries. Control is the catch: both mixed takes say it suits aggressive players, and Matthew K says it is for attackers and not patient dinking, and Pickleheads finds the loud pop makes dinks hard. Several prefer the 12.7 mm, though Pickleball Pursuit and JJ prefer the 14.3 mm.

Reviewers frame this Gen 1, non-thermoformed paddle as near Gen 3 power with more control, and Pickleheads calls it the best paddle Paddletek has made. Several say the 12.7 mm pops more than the 14.3 mm. Farmer Lanky, the one mixed take, finds the 12.7 really hard to control and says players who dink and play soft should skip it.

highlights.text: players who dink and play soft should skip it

paras: Reviewers recommend it to players who want maximum power, including those coming from tennis, and Cody Childers and STS both single out the 12.7 mm for power. The one mixed take says it is hard to control, very loud and weaker toward the edges, and prefers the lower swing weight TKO C. Another expects a fairly small sweet spot, and reset and block timing takes time to dial in.

highlights.text: single out the 12.7 mm for power

paras: Reviewers praise the spin and fast hands, and Farmer Lanky Pickleball and JJ Pickleball both rate the sweet spot as top tier or amazing for an edgeless paddle, while Famous by Friday Pickleball calls it pretty good but not huge and says slow swingers will probably not get on with it. Mixed takes come from Hdbnb, who reports dead spots on the sides, and from SupaSenpai, who gave it a 1.0 over price and a bulge at the bottom of the head after a month, whereas JJ Pickleball says durability needs more time and Hdbnb found it holding up apart from edge damage. On price, Hdbnb would probably choose the CRBN TruFoam 2 at a similar cost, and Farmer Lanky Pickleball could only recommend it at 160 to 220 dollars, though that reviewer and JJ Pickleball both disclose Proton discount codes.

highlights.text: bulge at the bottom of the head

paras: Most reviewers treat it as a budget elongated power paddle that needs weight, since the stock unit is light and unstable on off-center hits. Weighted, several put it close to but below the Selkirk Boomstick, and Pickleheads says it hits hard for a budget paddle. West Side, the one mixed take, calls the stock paddle average and tells anyone unwilling to add weight to skip it.

highlights.text: hits hard for a budget paddle
unwilling to add weight to skip it

paras: Reviewers like the R4 hybrid for its maneuverability and suit it to players willing to add weight, since several find the stock paddle thin, twitchy or short on power. Two reviewers say a weighted Quanta plays close to a Boomstick, though the Boomstick keeps an edge in peak power. The mixed take, from WhiskyDink, found the stock paddle flimsy and encourages players to try it stock first.

highlights.text: thin, twitchy or short on power

paras: Reviewers point this at advanced players and attackers who can control power, and the two positive takes both like the R4 shape. Two of the three mixed takes find the stock sweet spot tight, and two mention a stiff, tingy feel. Three reviewers add tungsten or throat weight to widen it.

Reviewers praise the spin and the soft, hollow feel, and the paddle suits players who value placement, resets and dinks over raw power, with Limitless Pickleball measuring it about 5 to 7 percent softer-hitting than the Q2. Mixed takes come mostly from grit durability and price: Pickleball Effect measured 96 percent of the grit roughness kept, while Johnkew Pickleball cited another tester's production units losing 350 to 400 RPM after about 50 games. Power ratings also disagree, with Pickleball Studio rating the 14 mm as low tier while JJ Pickleball found the 16 mm pop still high for touch shots.

highlights.text: pop still high for touch shots

paras: Reviewers mostly describe a light foam paddle that plays much like a Selkirk Boomstik, with big spin and power at a lower price, suited to aggressive players with a compact swing. Mixed takes center on the soft game and feel: Pickleheads and Pickleball Studio say resets take work, while Pickleball Playbook found soft shots easy to place, and Pickleball Willy reports an unpredictable hot spot near the center line. Grit durability also splits opinion, as The Sweet Spot Pickleball and Pickleball Studio say the texture wears quickly while Paddle Addicts saw no spin loss after about 10 hours.

highlights.text: plays much like a Selkirk Boomstik
unpredictable hot spot near the center line
no spin loss after about 10 hours

paras: Reviewers suit it to experienced, hard-hitting players, and both positive takes prefer the 10 mm Epic for control and faster hands. All three mixed takes center on a small, unforgiving sweet spot, and two reviewers call the face jarring, with one telling players prone to tennis elbow to pass. Pickleball Studio does not think it is worth $333 for most players.

Reviewers recommend it for players who want maximum power with a forgiving sweet spot, and one says it has the most power and pop of any paddle they have tested. Both mixed takes find the feel stiff and dislike the permanent MOI weights, and both say the cheaper SLK Era is easier to handle. Loose edge guards are reported in several takes.

Reviewers describe a dense, vibration-free foam filled feel, with no core crush reported by All Drive No Drop. Two reviewers place its power at the bottom of the power category, though one of them, Tickle My Pickleball, still calls it the best power paddle on the market right now. Johnkew, the one mixed take, finds the sweet spot feels small and suggests it for 4.5 players and above.

highlights.text: best power paddle on the market right now

paras: Reviewers pitch it as a budget power paddle with elite spin, and several call it a value standout. Both mixed takes are about the soft game: bepickleballer says drops, resets and dinks were not where it won them over, and a control player found the Enhance MPP Turbo easier to reset. Two lab wear tests showed spin losses of 13 to 15 percent.

highlights.text: not where it won them over

paras: Reviewers like it as a $100 foam paddle with durable-style grit, and Matthew K calls it an easy recommend. The mixed takes center on grit: Pickleball Studio measured spin falling nearly 29 percent after about 30 games, and Johnkew's wear test passed only narrowly. Pickleball Pursuit calls it a solid release that will not wow in any category, and Farmer Lanky warns players below 4.0 about control.

Most reviewers like it as a plusher, more forgiving take on the original Power series, with good dwell for resets and drops. Several say it plays much like that cheaper paddle, so the extra $30 buys feel rather than performance. One mixed take calls it too much power for beginners, and the other would only buy it at a real discount.

highlights.text: plays much like that cheaper paddle

paras: Reviewers split on feel. Pickleheads finds it stiff and hard to soften on dinks, while Johnkew calls it stiff and hollow with a narrower sweet spot. Pickleball Playbook calls it plush, dwelling and easy to place. Pickleheads recommends it for upper intermediate and advanced players who play a power game and want strong power for under $200.

highlights.text: plush, dwelling and easy to place

paras: Reviewers mostly like it as a stable all-court hybrid that handles dinks, drops and resets well, and several compare it with the Invader or the old Loco. Power is linear and not top of the market, so players wanting more should look elsewhere. The one mixed take finds it quick in the hand but says it does not carry players through resets.

highlights.text: does not carry players through resets

paras: Two of the three mixed takes call it a control paddle with a soft, dampened feel and limited pop, and one also finds low spin. The third finds thinner versions chaotic and prefers the 19 mm for consistency. WearTesters, the one positive review, instead finds strong pop on the elongated Pro 14 and likes its long handle.

The three reviewers split. Pickleball Blast likes it as a livelier, more predictable step up from the Genesis, while Pickleball Effect finds it rewards clean center contact but has dead zones near the top of the face until weight is added. Pickleball Studio says the sweet spot drop off stays severe even with added weight and calls it a hard pass at $280.

highlights.text: dead zones near the top of the face
sweet spot drop off stays severe

paras: Pickleball Nation likes the reach and leverage for two-handed backhands, and Pickleball Effect finds shotmaking precise and spinny on clean hits, but both say off-center hits are punished, and Effect adds dead zones near the top. Pickleball Studio, the one negative take, names the sweet spot the biggest problem, says added weight helps only a little and calls it a hard pass at $280.

All three reviewers like the pop and power, with a muted or plush feel. Rackets & Runners finds the sweet spot small and control a notch under most rivals, and Tickle My Pickleball finds the sweet spot and stability lacking. Rackets & Runners adds that the soft game gets little help. Pickleheads, a 5.0 player, still recommends it for advanced players, though it takes an adjustment period to avoid fliers.

highlights.text: the soft game gets little help

paras: Four reviewers praise the spin and a soft, dense or muted feel, with West Side and Pickleheads rating it high. Pickleball Playbook disagrees, finding at first that topspin drops rarely grab, with shots flying long or into the net. Power is modest, not a pure power paddle, and three reviewers say grit wear is unproven or unknown.

All three compare it with the Hyperion CFS 16, and two find it lighter and more controlled in the hand. Rackets & Runners and Pickleball Effect both say the grit wears faster, with Effect noting reduced grit after a couple of weeks. Famous by Friday, the one positive take, finds it forgiving and accurate but not a big spin paddle.

Reviewers mainly praise the spin, with three measuring around 2,200 RPM or more, plus power that stays predictable on a stable head. The heavy swing weight is the trade for three of them, making it slower in hand battles and less maneuverable at the net. Farmer Lanky, the one mixed take, finds it stiff and hard to control below 4.0.

Aggressive players who want a stiff paddle for put aways get the clearest fit, and reviewers praise the rougher face, with Pickleball Studio calling the grit the best part and JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Effect both measuring spin near 2,100 RPM. Takes split on feel, as Johnkew Pickleball found it the stiffest of 236 paddles while Famous by Friday described a plush ride with decent touch and sweet spot. Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Effect both found the sweet spot weak or small, and Pickleball Studio's added weight strips raised swing weight from 114 to 123 to improve power and stability.

Reviewers like it as a light, poppy widebody that is quick at the net, with several pointing to the low price. Feel is the disagreement: The Pickleball Reviews finds it plush with good touch, while Daniel Pickleball and Pickleball Studio find it stiff and poppy, so drops are harder to place. All Drive No Drop finds the power and pop sit below the Paddletek ESQ.

Reviewers mostly praise the soft, plush feel and the dwell that helps with dinks, drops and spin, and the paddle tends to suit higher level players who accept lower power and may add weight. Price and power draw the criticism, with Womack Pickleball and Kev Knows Pickleball both calling it hard to recommend at $250, while Pickle Li finds above average pop and gives it 7 out of 10. Sweet spot reports split, with Pickleheads calling it large and dependable and Womack Pickleball and Kev Knows Pickleball rating it below average or small.

All three reviewers find strong power from a light paddle, with a swing weight near 100 at Pickleheads and Pickleball Studio. Pickleball Portal also finds hand speed and midcourt volleys quicker than a 16mm paddle. Portal finds the sweet spot small and Studio below average. They split on soft shots: Portal finds dinks, resets and drops controllable, while Studio finds resets frustrating at first. Pickleheads adds that the edgeless face dinged in the first session.

highlights.text: hand speed and midcourt volleys quicker

paras: All three reviewers call the power top tier or extraordinary. DDOG Pickleball finds the wide body forgiving, and JJ Pickleball rates the sweet spot the largest of any power paddle. DDOG and Matt's Pickleball both add lead or tungsten tape to the very light stock weight. Matt's finds the extra pop makes mishits pop up higher, and JJ worries the power ends points within three shots.

highlights.text: the sweet spot the largest of any power paddle

paras: Reviewers agree it is among the most powerful paddles they tried, with maximum plow through on drives, serves and putaways. The shared trade is a 124 to 126 swing weight, which makes it slow in hand battles at the net, with a small sweet spot and low twist weight. Pickleball Medicine and Dash Pickleball are the most upbeat, though both still call it heavy.

highlights.text: slow in hand battles at the net

paras: Reviewers praise elite pop and power, with a big sweet spot on the widebody, and Pickleball Studio finds it plays almost like a Selkirk Boomstik. Control is the common trade: Pickleball Playbook says balls fly long once the swing extends, STS Pickleball calls control the catch, Pickleball Studio finds resets and drops the hardest part, and Pickle Li finds height harder to dial in. One TikTok creator likes the softer Jade better for kitchen control.

highlights.text: balls fly long once the swing extends
resets and drops the hardest part

paras: Reviewers rate it highly for players who want power with forgiveness, and Ontario Pickleball Academy calls it well rounded enough for beginners and elite players alike. Power is where takes differ: Pickle Li calls it mid-tier and Matt's Pickleball says to skip it for maximum raw power without modification, while Ontario Pickleball Academy finds the power easy to deploy though below Boomstick level. Pickle Li also reports some grit variance between units and core crushing concerns, and Ontario Pickleball Academy finds it head heavy from stock.

Reviewers focus on top-tier spin, around 2,265 to 2,293 RPM, and a very low swing weight that keeps the hands quick, with power rated mid to strong. The trade is a twist weight near 5.7, so three reviewers use lead tape or note twisting on off-center hits. BK Pickleball, the one mixed take, finds power exceptional but the sweet spot constricted.

Every take is mixed. Pickleball Effect measures elite power and very high spin but a small sweet spot, and a TikTok creator still reads it as a power paddle with a bigger sweet spot than the Black Opal. Pickle Li finds pop below average, with floated drops and a dead top of the face, and SupaSenpai calls it just okay on a handle-heavy unit.

Several reviewers find it the heaviest ball of the three Shift shapes, with dwell that helps touch shots. The split is stability: PickleTip gives it the lowest twist weight of the three shapes and Matt's Pickleball finds it the most sensitive on mishits, while STS Pickleball calls it their least favorite shape. Pickleball Medicine picks it as the favorite, with playable shots off the tip of the face.

Reviewers praise strong, predictable power and a big sweet spot at a price near or under $120, with Pickleball Effect measuring Tier 1 grit durability. Touch is the trade: Matt's Pickleball finds resets sit up and drops run long, Pickleball Playbook says drops took extra effort, and four reviewers call the feel stiff or hollow. Pickleball Pursuit calls the grit not durable.

Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Studio Clips loved the high spin and forgiving sweet spot at around $100, while Matt's Pickleball was mixed. Power is where takes split: Matt's Pickleball found it too poppy in stock form, Pickleball Studio called it a poppy power paddle, and Pickleball Studio Clips called it low tier power out of the box. Matt's Pickleball picks the elongated for anyone undecided, and grit loss ranged from 8 to 10% after 30 hours to 13% after 100 games.

highlights.text: high spin and forgiving sweet spot
low tier power out of the box

paras: Pickleball Union recommends the 16mm version to intermediate to advanced players with a tennis background, and Pickleball Playbook calls it a great singles paddle with effortless depth from the baseline. Control is where takes split: Pickleball Playbook finds resets and defensive drops poor, with balls dumping into the net, while Pickleball Union rates control as one of the strongest parts. Dink n Drive, on the 14mm 2026 edition, likes the spin but says other paddles offer more value at about $300.

Reviewers praise the spin and its durability on this light 16mm hybrid, and Pickleball Playbook and Matt's Pickleball also like the easy soft game. Opinions split on power and sweet spot: Farmer Lanky Pickleball puts power at the bottom of its category, while Pickleball Playbook calls it very powerful, and Pickleball Studio and JJ Pickleball found the sweet spot average or weak off-center at stock weight. Several reviewers add tape to steady it, though Pickleball Studio disliked half gram tungsten tape at the head and bottom corners.

Reviewers praised the pop, spin and drives, with Pickle Li, who also posts on MyPickleList, calling it a mid-tier power paddle that plays well stock, while The Pickleball Pirates placed it in the upper third for power. Mixed takes come from feel and sweet spot: West Side Pickleball found it muted with a narrower sweet spot than the Hyperion, Pickleball Playbook said the sweet spot is not massive, and Matt's Pickleball called $260 a tough sell. Matt's Pickleball and The Pickleball Pirates both preferred the 16mm over the 14mm.

highlights.text: muted with a narrower sweet spot

paras: Reviewers praise strong pop, spin and a plush feel, and it suits players who want power without losing touch. Most find the 14mm more aggressive with more pop, while Pickleball Pursuit and Johnkew Pickleball find the 16mm softer with less pop. Stock weight splits opinion, as Pickleball Effect and Famous by Friday Pickleball add weight while Johnkew Pickleball found it easy to play stock, and the price is called high by Famous by Friday Pickleball but fair by Pickleball Union.

highlights.text: strong pop, spin and a plush feel

paras: Reviewers praise the Zen S+ for easy power at a swing weight around 107 and a very large sweet spot, and Pickleball Effect ranked it first for power in a group of MPP foam paddles. Opinions split on pop and spin: Pickleball Effect and Not Dead Yet Pickleball found pop low, Pickleball Playbook called spin average, and SupaSenpai said the production paddle shipped with less grit than early units, while Matthew K Pickleball found spin very good. Not Dead Yet Pickleball, the one mixed take, found a flat spot near the throat and would choose the 11SIX24 Ultre.

Reviewers praise the huge, forgiving sweet spot and control of the widebody, and recommend it for beginners and control-minded players on a budget. Power is the common limit: RYE3D Printing found many drives die before the back of the court, and STS Pickleball measured soft power and pop well below average. Takes differ on spin and wear, as Pickleheads called the spin strong for fiberglass and expects it to hold up, while STS Pickleball says the raw carbon face loses grit as it wears smooth.

highlights.text: many drives die before the back of the court
soft power and pop well below average

paras: Pickleball Playbook loved the 16mm widebody, citing a big sweet spot and very controlled drops and resets, and picked it for most players below roughly 5.0. Farmer Lanky Pickleball was mixed, finding control harder below 5.0 or coming from foam paddles, and called the sweet spot average and the $300 price overpriced. Pickleball Studio found a softer feel after break-in but would buy a Pro 4 at $229 or $250 instead, and says core crushing remains a risk.

Reviewers praise the power, pop and a roomy sweet spot, with Cody Childers and Pickleball Medicine both loving it and Johnkew Pickleball picking it as the most forgiving of the three shapes. Takes turn mixed on weight and control: Pickleball Studio finds the sweet spot tight and the paddle slow for a widebody, All Drive No Drop thinks the sweet spot is about average, and Pickleball Tech Dude says resets are hard to soften. Three reviewers prefer the R4 hybrid over this shape, and Johnkew Pickleball notes that EVA foam durability is unproven.

Reviewers praise the Integra XL for a very quiet, dampened feel and a mix of forgiveness and maneuverability, with Matt's Pickleball, Briones Pickleball Breakdown and Pickleball Pursuit all liking it. Mixed takes come mostly from the sweet spot and the stock setup: Pickleball Studio rated the sweet spot subpar stock and Pickleball Medicine found it average to slightly small, while Briones called it huge. Pickleheads found it head-heavy and pricey, and named the Six Zero DBD Control as a better all-rounder for almost $100 less.

Reviewers mostly praise the quick hands, spin and easy dinks, drops and resets at $119, and it suits all-court players. Power is where takes split: Pickleheads calls it the best power paddle under $150 they have played, while Amir's Pickleball and Spinwave Pickleball say power is not its strength, and STS Pickleball rates control as its weakest score. Grit life is the common worry, with The New Main Pickleball seeing wear near the center after about 10 hours and Spinwave Pickleball reporting the grit wore off after the first day.

highlights.text: quick hands, spin and easy dinks
grit wore off after the first day

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the quiet sound with strong power and pop, and Famous by Friday Pickleball and Pickleball Portal both say the soft foam face suits sore arms. Takes split on control: Kev Knows Pickleball and To Pickleball & Beyond found it hard to dial back, while Famous by Friday Pickleball and Pickleball Portal describe a trampoline feel that settles once the swing is calibrated, and Pickleball Union reports control coming together by the second and third games. To Pickleball & Beyond and Famous by Friday Pickleball also both compare it with the Diadem Vice and see the Hush as the more controllable of the two.

highlights.text: quiet sound with strong power and pop

paras: Reviewers who liked it point to more control and a bigger sweet spot than the Pro Power, with Pickleball Portal and JJ Pickleball the most positive. Mixed takes come from weight: Pickleball Effect, Matthew K Pickleball and Johnkew Pickleball all call it heavy, head heavy or sluggish in stock form, and Matthew K prefers the original Pro Power Elongated for its fast hands at the kitchen. Pickleball Effect and Johnkew Pickleball added tungsten tape, which lowered the balance point and left it feeling more stable or no heavier.

highlights.text: more control and a bigger sweet spot

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the Quartz for soft-game control, a plush feel and a light swing weight at around $90, and several suggest it for beginners or a first upgrade. Sweet spot size is where takes split: BK Pickleball and The Pickleball Pirates call it huge, while STS Pickleball calls it very tight and Pickleheads finds it small for a square shape. STS Pickleball also recommends the Six Zero Ruby or Double Black Diamond over it, and reviewers agree power is low, with several mentioning lead tape as an adjustment.

Reviewers praise the strong power and spin for a fiberglass face, and the weight of about 8 ounces helps in fast hand battles at the net. Takes turn mixed on the soft game: Pickleheads found the feel very stiff and popped up drops and dinks, Pickleball Effect said the soft game took a solid week to settle, and Tickle My Pickleball found drops and resets harder than on a Vatic V7. Comparisons also differ, as Pickleheads put the power close to the Selkirk Vanguard Power Air Invikta, Pickleball Effect said it falls a little short of a Selkirk Power Air, and Pickleheads recommends the Double Black Diamond Control over it for nearly every player.

highlights.text: took a solid week to settle

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the hybrid shape for its low swing weight, quick hands at the net and strong spin, with Pickleball Blast and Matt's Pickleball both measuring swing weights around 107. Mixed takes come from price and from players already on an earlier shape: Pickleball Studio calls the Honolulu J2NF the better paddle overall, and Pickleball Tech Dude doubts it is worth trying for players who already own a one through three shape. Several reviewers also add tungsten or lead tape because the stock sweet spot is smaller than some rivals.

Reviewers mostly describe an aggressive spin and power paddle, with Pickleheads rating the spin among the best they have tested. Takes split on the sweet spot and power: PickleTip found a large, forgiving sweet spot, while Pickleball Effect found a small sweet spot and less power than the Paddletek Bantam and JOOLA Pro IV. Several reviewers also found the head-heavy balance slow at the net and preferred the thinner 12.7mm there.

highlights.text: head-heavy balance slow at the net

paras: Reviewers praise the Perseus 3S Dual for control and a stable feel, with The Raw Reviews recommending the 16mm version to intermediate to advanced players who want reach and a premium feel, and vonEgypt Pickleball seeing the 14mm as a cheaper, easier alternative to the Pro 4. Takes differ on power: Dink n Drive found somewhat less power than the original Perseus 3S and called slice spin only okay, while vonEgypt Pickleball noted a slight drop in power and pop against the Pro 4. Dink n Drive saw no crushed core after roughly 150 to 200 hours, though one Reddit player reported a cracking noise from the core after around three months.

Reviewers praise the soft, dense feel and the extra pop of the 16mm widebody, with Matt's Pickleball finding the sweet spot big and consistent and Johnkew Pickleball calling the R2 the safest pick for most players. Takes split on forgiveness, as Pickleball Effect measured a 6.62 twist weight against a 7.25 widebody average and struggled to control it, while Spinwave Pickleball rated the sweet spot slightly above average for the shape. Matt's Pickleball also reported that their R2 delaminated after hours of drilling in 90 to 95 degree heat, though the other three shapes held up.

Reviewers praise the spin and the soft, dense feel that makes resets, drops and dinks easy, and it suits players who bring their own pace. Opinions split on stability: Pickleball Playbook found it top heavy with the sweet spot far from the hand, and MyPickleList found a smaller sweet spot in stock form but more stability with 3 g added at 3 and 9 o'clock, while Matt's Pickleball called the sweet spot large. Several reviewers prefer the Ultre, though Pickleball Effect picked the Vapor over it.

Reviewers praise the Hybrid-W as a quick, stable paddle with easy blocks and resets, with Pickleball Effect measuring a 107 swing weight and The Pickleball Reviews 107.4. Most comparisons are against the Pakle Fuse Elongated, which reviewers describe as having more power and reach, while PaddleCompare (Johnny Pickleball) found the Hybrid-W better for control and resets, though from separate sessions rather than head-to-head play. Grit durability draws the most caution: Pickleball Effect rated it top, but Matthew K Pickleball and The Pickleball Reviews both mention earlier batches with problems and say the latest needs more time.

Reviewers mostly praise the pop and pace, along with a sweet spot that several call large for an elongated shape, and Pickleball Willy, Pickleball Playbook Paddles, SNPickleball and Spinwave Pickleball all loved it. The mixed takes come from the soft game: Nico the Lefty said it punishes drops and resets, STS Pickleball said dinks float, and Spinwave Pickleball expects a short adjustment period for players coming from control paddles. Against the Cyclone Hybrid, Pickleball Willy and Nico the Lefty found the elongated more powerful, while WhiskyDink found the two play much alike.

highlights.text: sweet spot that several call large

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the 13mm elongated Halo Power for extra pop over the 16mm Control XL with little control lost, and three call the sweet spot large or massive. Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Effect are the mixed voices, with Pickleball Studio finding resets at the kitchen harder and balls sitting up, and adding lead tape for stability, a step that several other reviewers also mention. Spin readings of 1400 to 1450 RPM from Pickleball Portal and Pickleballogist fall below other raw carbon paddles that reach 1600 RPM.

highlights.text: extra pop over the 16mm Control XL
fall below other raw carbon paddles

paras: The hybrid Barrage 4 suits players who want fast hands, spin and put-away power, and West Side Pickleball, The Honest Take and Pickleheads all liked it, though several reviewers added weight to settle it. Takes split on the sweet spot and pop: West Side Pickleball calls the sweet spot the best of any 14mm they have played, while MyPickleList finds it below average to average in stock form and rates power as mid-tier. Reviewers who also played the standard Barrage 2 call it the more forgiving shape, with the 4 being the spicier one.

highlights.text: fast hands, spin and put-away power
below average to average in stock form

paras: Reviewers who liked it point to spin and controlled power for aggressive players who can hit the center, with the 2 and 4 shapes picked most often. Takes split on power: Pickleheads put it near the top of the market, while Farmer Lanky Pickleball placed it at the bottom of the power category and Pickleball Tech Dude found the gain over the Genesis too small. Every reviewer criticizes the small sweet spot, and several also object to the $280 price.

Reviewers praise the widebody for a very large sweet spot, a forgiving feel and usable power, and it suits players wanting a forgiving power paddle or a step up from control paddles. Takes differ on pop: Pickleball Effect calls it medium pop and more all court, while Pickleball Studio finds it notably poppier than the Vapor and Hurache-X, and RYE3D Printing and Pickleball Studio both found resets needed adjusting. Johnkew Pickleball and STS PICKLEBALL both preferred the Vapor, and PickleTip, the one mixed take on the original generation, advises buying only at a clear discount.

highlights.text: buying only at a clear discount

paras: Reviewers praise the soft, dense feel and the spin and control it gives for resets, drops and dinks, and it suits players who generate their own pace. Mixed takes come mostly from power and weight: Pickleball Playbook picks it as the paddle they trust most in a tournament, while West Side Pickleball found a flat sound and heavier feel and would pay for the Power 2 instead. Pickleball Effect and STS Pickleball both note a heavy swing weight that slows hands at the kitchen, and each lists it as UPA-A approved but not USA Pickleball approved.

Reviewers who liked it point to strong power from an elongated shape that does not feel sluggish, with Pickleball Effect and Johnkew Pickleball both playing it without added weight. Mixed takes come from the sweet spot: Matthew K Pickleball found it bigger than the Vapor's, while Pickleball Effect, STS PICKLEBALL and PickleTip found it tighter or narrower. Johnkew Pickleball and STS PICKLEBALL both preferred the Vapor, and Pickleball Tech Dude rated this the most powerful but least poppy of the three.

highlights.text: strong power from an elongated shape

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the widebody Shift for quick hands, strong spin and a forgiving sweet spot, and it suits players who want control with moderate power. Matt's Pickleball gave the mixed take, finding the feel too dense and muted for their taste, and STS Pickleball also called it denser than the plush feel others report. Power comparisons vary: Farmer Lanky Pickleball places it between the Honolulu NF series and the Loco, while Pickleheads says the Loco offers more power out of the box.

Reviewers who liked it point to the 18K carbon face for spin and the power that comes with it: Famous by Friday Pickleball liked the plush, large sweet spot on the 16mm, and Tickle My Pickleball rated spin top tier. Opinions split on feel, since Tickle My Pickleball found the elongated Pro stiff until about a week of break-in, while Pickleball Addict Life found the soft game less forgiving and preferred the livelier JOOLA Perseus Pro IV 16 it used as a benchmark. Famous by Friday Pickleball also called the $249.95 price steep for an EP foam paddle.

Reviewers praise the plush, soft feel and spin, and it suits players who want touch with a little more power than the original LUXX. Johnkew Pickleball and Pickleball Effect measured a low stock twist weight (5.9 and 5.83), and Pickleball Nation found the narrower face less forgiving, while West Side Pickleball rated the sweet spot as very generous. Pickleball Effect called the $280 price hard to justify, whereas West Side Pickleball thought it probably warranted.

Reviewers who liked it were mostly after spin and control, with Rackets & Runners and All Drive No Drop pointing to Kevlar plushness and soft touch, and Pickleball Medicine noting a consistent face feel. Takes on power split against the Mach Forza: Pickleball Medicine and Farmer Lanky found slightly more pop and power than the Mach 1 Forza, while The Pickleball Pirates found less power and spin than the Mach line, and All Drive No Drop found power and pop lacking. Control is also mixed, as Rackets & Runners found it better for control but less consistent than the Mach 1 Forza, and Farmer Lanky found it harder to handle.

Reviewers praise the pop, the $200 price and the one-year warranty, with Johnkew Pickleball and Pickleball Studio both calling the sweet spots generous or top tier. Takes split on power and shape: Pickleball Effect and Matt's Pickleball call the elongated 16mm an all-court paddle rather than a power paddle, Pickle Li puts the 16mm widebody at lower to mid tier power, and Pickleheads and Pickleball Willy find the elongated sweet spot tight or smaller than the widebody. Resets and drops feel harder at first for some, as West Side Pickleball struggled with resets and The Pickleball Pirates found the stiff face jarring on resets.

highlights.text: all-court paddle rather than a power paddle

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the 16mm for a soft feel, easy control on resets and drops, and a quicker swing than the Hyperion, with Rackets & Runners calling it the softest and most controlled thermoformed paddle it tried. Takes split on price and power: The Pickleball Pirates call $250 a good buy while Farmer Lanky Pickleball would not recommend it at $250, and Derik Hyndman finds more pop than the Hyperion while Pickleball Effect and Rackets & Runners find less power than other thermoformed paddles. Famous by Friday Pickleball, STS Pickleball and Briones Pickleball Academy all point to a smaller sweet spot that hurts on off-center hits.

highlights.text: softest and most controlled thermoformed paddle

paras: Reviewers mostly praise a dense, plush feel, a large sweet spot and easy all-court control across the X, S and V shapes. Comparisons with the Pulse split on pop: Womack Pickleball and Tickle My Pickleball found slightly more pop, while DDOG_Pickleball found the Pulse hotter and the Harmony more controllable. Mixed takes come from price and power, with Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Effect questioning $180 against cheaper rivals, and vonEgypt Pickleball finding baseline power short in about three hours of play.

Reviewers mostly suit it to players who liked the original Loco and want the same stiff, hollow feel with more spin and grit that lasts, and Pickleball Studio measured spin holding through 117 games. Mixed takes come from control, as STS Pickleball leans toward the Hybrid for most players because the Elongated has a smaller sweet spot, and PickleTip picks the Hybrid by a small margin because the Elongated is less forgiving off-center. Axel Lee Pickleball and Johnkew Pickleball both warn that the springy pop makes midcourt resets hard, and Johnkew ran their grit wear test on a Hybrid only.

highlights.text: more spin and grit that lasts
springy pop makes midcourt resets hard

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the power and pop, with vonEgypt Pickleball rating counters at Paddletek level or better and Famous by Friday Pickleball measuring a 52.6 mph serve against a normal serve near 50. Mixed takes come from durability, where Pickleball Studio and Pickleball Pursuit point to bad looking X-rays and crushed or compressed core cells and suggest waiting, and from feel, where Paddle Addicts found it head heavy with jarring off-center hits after adding weight while vonEgypt Pickleball found the sweet spot covers most of the paddle. Pickleball Pursuit and Paddle Addicts both preferred it to the Metallic T.

highlights.text: counters at Paddletek level or better

paras: Reviewers who loved it, Pickleball Studio, STS Pickleball and Johnkew Pickleball among them, point to a large sweet spot, and Johnkew Pickleball adds better control than most power paddles. District Pickleball and RYE3D Printing were mixed, finding drives hard to dial in stock, with RYE3D Printing saying weight on the top corners helped, and RYE3D Printing and STS Pickleball both place its power below other Power series paddles. PickleTip tested the original version and found it the most balanced of the three Power shapes, but suggests newer generations when prices are close.

Reviewers mostly praise the Hybrid for control, a consistent sweet spot and spin from the 18K carbon face, and MyPickleList says it works in stock form without mods. Feel is where takes split: Tickle My Pickleball finds it the stiffest of any Gen 4 paddles and Pickle Li and MyPickleList call it firm, while The Pickleball Pirates describe a plush face with a wide sweet spot. Power also varies, with Tickle My Pickleball rating pop high, especially on the 14mm, while Pickle Li, MyPickleList and Pickleball Portal place it below paddles such as the RPM or Boomstik.

highlights.text: below paddles such as the RPM or Boomstik

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the power, and Pickleheads, All Drive No Drop and WhiskyDink lean toward the 16mm widebody for more control and a softer feel than the 14mm. Mixed takes come from touch and feel: Francis Rances found the 14mm too powerful for a control game, Paddle Addicts kept the 16mm as a backup because of a stiffer face and less drive power, and STS Pickleball called its pop very low while WhiskyDink noted high pop at the kitchen. The short 5.25 inch handle was criticized by All Drive No Drop and STS Pickleball, and WhiskyDink pointed out the $280 price.

highlights.text: too powerful for a control game

paras: Reviewers praise the spin, with Pickleheads calling it the best spin of any paddle right now, vonEgypt Pickleball rating the grit top tier, and PB HEAT adding a wide sweet spot and stable resets. Takes split on power: Pickleheads finds less raw baseline power than the Selkirk Boomstik, PB HEAT places it in the low to mid-range of power paddles, and vonEgypt Pickleball rates the power right up there, while PB HEAT also found the square stock handle painful until regripping it. Pickleheads warns the grit will wear over time, and PB HEAT doubts the surface is durable.

highlights.text: best spin of any paddle right now

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the power and a very large sweet spot, which suits attackers more than soft game players, and several reviewers warn that the pop makes soft shots harder to control. Opinions split on value and spin: Matt's Pickleball cannot recommend it at $333 because similar performance costs less, while Pickleball Effect measured below-average spin at 1,980 RPM against about 2,300 from Johnkew Pickleball and STS Pickleball. Edge guard loosening or lifting comes up in several reviews, though some cases involved the elongated shape or removed weights.

highlights.text: makes soft shots harder to control

paras: Reviewers who like it point to the quick hand speed, and Matthew K Pickleball picked the 14mm as the most well-rounded for pop, feel and spin. Pickleball Studio and Matt's Pickleball both found the sweet spot small in stock form, especially on the 12.7mm, and all four reviewers either added weight or said it needs it. SupaSenpai, on a 16mm demo with no weight allowed, found less control than the original C45 and called it too expensive.

highlights.text: sweet spot small in stock form

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the large sweet spot, the pop and the spin, and it suits players who want compact offense at the net. Mixed takes come from sibling comparisons: Pickleball Playbook and The Pickleball Reviews rank the J2CR ahead, and Wongsquared would probably pick the J6 and found fast dinks hard to control. Grit durability is disputed, with West Side Pickleball noting no durable grit surface while The Pickleball Reviews calls Blue Grit durable.

Reviewers mostly praise the soft, plush feel, the large sweet spot and the control on dinks, drops and resets, with several recommending it for all court play. Takes split on spin and pop: Scooter Reviews Stuff rates spin as top tier and Pickleheads calls it elite, while STS Pickleball found less grip on rolls, Daniel Pickleball calls spin good but not amazing, and Farmer Lanky Pickleball puts pop in the lower tier. STS Pickleball and Pickleheads gave the two mixed ratings, citing a harder drop off outside the sweet spot and a heavy, slow feel at the net.

Reviewers praise the EPP Turbo as a budget power paddle with a large sweet spot, and Pickleball Playbook and Austin Hardy both say frame hits and shanks still go in. Mixed takes come from comparisons: STS Pickleball and The Pickleball Reviews both prefer the MPP Turbo, while Pickleball Tech Dude and Pickleball Studio Clips each put it at about 90% of the Bread & Butter Loco for far less money. Opinions on the hybrid shape split, with All Drive No Drop saying its smaller face hurts returns and resets, while Pickleball Tech Dude preferred it to the Loco hybrid.

highlights.text: smaller face hurts returns and resets

paras: Reviewers praise the plush, dense feel, long dwell time and forgiving control, with several calling it an all-court paddle that suits players who want touch over loud pop. Takes turn mixed on power and shape: Matt's Pickleball and Pickleball Blast find power modest next to the Loco or Boomstick, while Johnkew Pickleball finds all three shapes hit harder than the Harmony. The X elongated draws swing weight concerns, with Johnkew Pickleball measuring 123.5 and TIM Z reporting 121 to 123, and Matt's Pickleball never got on with the V widebody, while Pickleball Medicine names the V a personal favorite.

highlights.text: power modest next to the Loco

paras: Reviewers mostly describe it as a fit for players who want control with some power, especially those who found the Boomstick too hot or too head heavy. Takes split on how much is given up: Pickleball Advocate found better control than the Boomstick and Nikki Maldonado called control the standout, while Johnkew Pickleball, the one mixed rating, found firepower clearly lower, a slightly smaller sweet spot and less instant pop on flicks and counters. Shape also matters, since The Pickleball Dad doubts the elongated suits many players and Johnkew Pickleball prefers the widebody, and Pickle Li and Pickleball Advocate both say a new unit needs a break-in.

Reviewers praise the power and pop, a light and maneuverable swing for an elongated shape, and a stable sweet spot, with JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Tech Dude both singling out the even feel from center to edges. Takes split on feel and control: Maiko finds little dwell and a stiff, hollow feel that suits bangers, while Wongsquared found the touch very good after a slightly stiff start and Scooters and Pickleball TV found it easy to control. Grit is the main concern, as Maiko, JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Tech Dude each report spin falling over time, while Wongsquared and Scooters and Pickleball TV say its lifespan is still unproven.

Reviewers praise the large sweet spot and the spin, and STS Pickleball says it suits aggressive players who attack, while Paddle Addicts points to Loco 1 users looking to upgrade. Power is where takes split: Paddle Addicts calls it mid tier, while STS Pickleball calls it a power paddle first and Pickleball Playbook Paddles calls it very powerful. Control and weight also vary, since STS Pickleball finds resets need softer hands, Pickleball Playbook Paddles finds resets easy with no need to add weight, and Paddle Addicts and STS Pickleball both say it has room for added weight.

Reviewers praise a soft, forgiving feel with strong control and spin, and the paddle suits players who value touch over raw power. Power is where takes split: UnforcedErrorsPB and The Paddle Plug describe it as giving up some pop and lacking instant explosiveness, while Matthew K Pickleball found it poppier than the J2NF and muted the pop because soft hits launched upward. Dwell Time Pickleball prefers it to the J2NF for pocketing the ball more, though they rated power on the lower end of the range.

Reviewers praise the sweet spot and the softer feel compared with the 8M, and Pickleball Pursuit says it suits players wanting power with easy control. Mixed takes come from price and break-in: Pickleball Tech Dude warns of a break-in of 15 to 25 plus games on the elongated shape, while Womack Pickleball sees no break-in yet and finds it hard to recommend next to the Sparta Spitfire at nearly $150 less. Johnkew Pickleball adds that the power hides at first, causing long serves and drives, and that not everyone will see a return on nearly $300.

Reviewers who want Boomstik power praise the extra spin from the InfiniGrit Ultra face, and STS Pickleball measured 2,419 RPM against 2,305 for the original elongated. Takes on control differ, as Pickleball Advocate found it less poppy and easier to manage than the original, while Ty Butson said it is not a control paddle and Axel Lee found resets the hardest part. Grit wear is another question, since Axel Lee felt the face go smoother after 20 hours and STS Pickleball reported early units going smooth, which Selkirk called a manufacturing defect.

highlights.text: extra spin from the InfiniGrit Ultra face

paras: Reviewers praise the added power over the original J2Ti, big spin and a large sweet spot, and Famous by Friday Pickleball suggests it suits spin players who accept a break-in period. Mixed takes come from control and break-in: Famous by Friday found a stiff, harsh early stage and control that needs searching for, while To Pickleball & Beyond found slightly less control than the Ti and more jump on dinks and drops. DY Pickleball had not played it yet and was disappointed that Gen 3 durability is traded for power.

highlights.text: added power over the original J2Ti
slightly less control than the Ti

paras: Reviewers liked this elongated paddle as a light base for players who plan to add weight, with Matt's Pickleball measuring 2,480 RPM and vonEgypt Pickleball finding it very maneuverable. Reviewers describe stock power as low, and Matt's Pickleball found blocks get pushed around until weight is added, while Farmer Lanky Pickleball found control very good for 3.5 players and up. Farmer Lanky Pickleball also says the peel ply grit is not durable, and the sweet spot is described as respectable by one reviewer and average by another.

highlights.text: peel ply grit is not durable

paras: Salt N Pepper Pickleball and CarpeDink'em Pickleball both rated it highly for a soft, plush feel and a large sweet spot that stays consistent on off-center hits. Power is where takes differ: Salt N Pepper Pickleball called it power first for players who swing fully, while CarpeDink'em Pickleball put it at the bottom of the power range and not too poppy. TGu was mixed, finding stock stability lacking on return of serve, adding weight at 3:00 and 9:00 to help, and still would not play it in a tournament.

Reviewers praise strong power on full swings from a light, maneuverable hybrid paddle, and it suits players who swing through the ball. Mixed takes come from the soft game: JJ Pickleball found very low pop on slow shots and advises against it for players who rely on the paddle when dinking, while EZY3D LAB found dinks and resets controlled. Pickleball Effect ranked it first for power but last for pop against four other MPP foam paddles, and views on grit durability differ, with EZY3D LAB expecting wear and JJ Pickleball seeing it hold up.

highlights.text: very low pop on slow shots

paras: The M105 suits players who want a soft, controlled paddle for drops, resets and dinks, and Paddle Review Hub and Matt's Pickleball both came away fond of it. Takes split on power: Paddle Review Hub found plenty on full swings, while West Side Pickleball rated it the weakest of the three it compared, and Matt's Pickleball got no power until adding side strips. Matthew K Pickleball also found low pop and said firefights feel like a disadvantage, and West Side Pickleball does not see it as a fit for aggressive net players.

highlights.text: no power until adding side strips

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the spin and power, and the paddle suits offensive players who like a stiff, hollow feel. Mixed takes come from who it fits and how it is weighted: Farmer Lanky recommends it to 4.0 and higher players and warns casual 3.5 players off, while Pickleball Tech Dude sees it suiting casual or average players but finds it heavy with little room for customization. Shape matters too, as Johnkew Pickleball picks the widebody as most well-rounded and Farmer Lanky finds the hybrid sweet spot and twist weight lag.

Reviewers praise the spin and controllable pace. Royal Pickleball and Nate Nalven both suit it to players wanting an all court power paddle without boom stick power, while RALLYHAUS PICKLEBALL points it at intermediate to advanced players and warns beginners may find it frustrating. Power is where takes split: Royal Pickleball and Nate Nalven put it around seven and a half, a little above the widebody and below the RPM Q2, but RALLYHAUS PICKLEBALL calls it low-tier overall, with a dead center hot spot that sent serves and returns long, and also reports arm fatigue after the first few hours.

highlights.text: arm fatigue after the first few hours

paras: Reviewers mostly praise the added power over the J2K while the sweet spot and spin stay strong, and DY Pickleball now uses it as a main paddle. Mixed takes come from the extra pop and durability: DY Pickleball found dinks and resets out of the air harder to control, STS PICKLEBALL rated control slightly below the original, and Pickle Techie reported core crush after over a month while DY Pickleball heard none after two months. To Pickleball & Beyond judged power close to the J2 TI Plus on first impressions only, and said the TI Plus currently hits harder.

highlights.text: sweet spot and spin stay strong
core crush after over a month

paras: The GTO-C suits players who want pop and power and can live with a tight sweet spot, and Pickleball Pursuit and Pickleball Studio each name it a favorite among Paddletek models. Pickle Li was more mixed, calling it a mid-tier power paddle that is less forgiving on dinks and resets, while Johnkew rated the 12.7mm in the elite power tier. The 14.3mm comes across as more muted and easier to use, and JJ Pickleball and Pickleball Studio both flag a high swing weight for a hybrid.

highlights.text: less forgiving on dinks and resets

paras: Reviewers praise a light, stable full foam paddle with a large sweet spot that suits players wanting power without losing touch. Takes split on pop and spin: Pickleball Rx gave pop 9 out of 10 and warned the sound is loud, while The Sweet Spot Pickleball called pop low and spin very good but not the best, and WhiskyDink rated spin as elite. Grit durability is the open question, since Mid-Century Pickleball and The Sweet Spot Pickleball could not confirm it, and Mid-Century Pickleball notes the next batch changes the grit.

Reviewers who liked it point to power and spin, with Royal Pickleball finding the elongated 15mm version very light with effortless power and plenty of spin, and Famous by Friday Pickleball rating control and spin very good on centered hits. The sweet spot is the main split: Royal Pickleball called it large and forgiving for an elongated shape, while Famous by Friday Pickleball called it small and All Drive No Drop Pickleball found it not the best out of the box. Price and grit also draw comment, as Famous by Friday Pickleball called $195 pricey and All Drive No Drop Pickleball noted no durable grit at about $180 after discount.

highlights.text: effortless power and plenty of spin

paras: Reviewers praise the forgiving feel, with The Volley Zone and vonEgypt Pickleball both finding the widebody 16mm version very stable on off-center hits, and Famous by Friday Pickleball liking the soft touch at the net. Mixed takes come from price and comparisons: Tickle My Pickleball calls it a budget 008 with MOI weights rather than a budget Boomstick and questions the $180 price, while Famous by Friday Pickleball says Boomstick or Era Power players should stay put and a cheaper game improvement paddle is probably available. Limited power is the shared drawback, and Famous by Friday Pickleball adds that swinging hard makes it worse.

Reviewers praise the Draco Hybrid for pop and power, and it suits players wanting a light, customizable hybrid for offense. Takes split on the sweet spot, which Pickleball Tech Dude calls extremely large, while Pickleball Studio rates it about average and Pickle Li says it is not way bigger than normal. Pickleball Studio also finds it hard to control for all-court or low power players and calls it good but not a standout.

Reviewers mostly praise the J3NF for quick hands at the net, a low swing weight and a great sweet spot, with ThomasFL calling it the best standard paddle and All Drive No Drop Pickleball naming it a top pick for an offensive widebody. Takes differ on power: ThomasFL puts it at roughly 85% of the Loco, while Tickle My Pickleball and All Drive No Drop Pickleball call it the poppiest of their comparison groups. The Pickleball Pirates prefer elongated faces and say the shorter face takes getting used to, and Tickle My Pickleball says it gives up some reach next to the original J2NF.

Reviewers mostly point this paddle at players who want a soft, controlled feel, with Pickleball Medicine and All Drive No Drop both praising a forgiving sweet spot and strong stability. Opinions split on how much power is enough: Matt's Pickleball finds it noticeably less powerful than the Kevlar model and possibly too muted for players coming from bouncier paddles, while Pickleball Medicine sees it as a fit for players moving up to power paddles who do not want full pop. Two reviewers preferred the carbon J2 NF, and swing weight readings vary, from very low at Pickleball Medicine to 115.5 at Matt's Pickleball.
